metadata.title: Why do East Asian students do so well in mathematics? A machine learning study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics data for five East Asian economies (students, teachers, and principals) and constructs a student-level prediction dataset with 22 socio-ecological predictors. The manuscript reports handling of missing data via MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26.0 and then fits a random forest regression model in R. It does not report applying TIMSS complex-sample student/sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the ML approach is implemented as a single-level fixed-effect random forest despite the nested TIMSS structure (students within classes/schools within economies). As a result, the analysis likely treats observations as effectively unweighted for population-representativeness and does not explicitly propagate the complex survey design uncertainty into the ML performance estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics assessment data restricted to five East Asian economies: Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, and Singapore. The analytic dataset focuses on student-level mathematics achievement (number, algebra, geometry, and data/probability domains) and includes predictors available in TIMSS 2019 student, teacher, and principal questionnaires, mapped to socio-ecological individual, microsystem, and mesosystem factors. Missingness across variables was handled with MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26.0 (missing completely at random; 0–5.7% missing depending on variable). The random forest regression was run separately for each of the five mathematics plausible values and the final estimate was the mean across the five PV-specific models.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (five East Asian economies: Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (single-level); 10-fold cross-validation with 5 repeats. Whole East Asian sample: R²=0.49, RMSE=0.71; top-11 predictors model: R²=0.49, RMSE=0.71 (MSE decreased to 0.53 for top-11 set). Candidate-set performance (mean decreased MSE): Top 1=0.78, Top 3=0.66, Top 6=0.59, Top 11=0.53, Top 22=0.52.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, and Singapore, the study leveraged students’ confidence in mathematics, student SES, and school emphasis on academic success (plus teaching limitations and students’ value of mathematics) to predict mathematics achievement, finding that the top-11 socio-ecological variables explained 49% of the variance (R²=0.49) with RMSE=0.71 under random forest regression. This indicates that strengthening students’ mathematics confidence and aligning school-level academic success expectations—alongside targeted support for disadvantaged students—may be high-leverage levers for improving mathematics outcomes, though the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics data from five East Asian economies (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore; N=21,340 students) and predicts mathematics achievement (number, algebra, geometry, and data/probability domains) using a random forest regression model. Missing data were handled with MCMC multiple imputation (0–5.7% missing across variables), and plausible values were addressed by running separate models for each of the five mathematics PVs and averaging the results. In the omnibus East Asian sample, the final top-11 predictor set achieved R²=0.49 and RMSE=0.71, with mean decreased MSE dropping to 0.53 after the 11th variable during 10-fold cross-validation with five repeats. The most important predictors were students’ confidence in mathematics, student SES, and school emphasis on academic success. Limitations include the use of single-level random forest despite TIMSS’s nested design and the absence of reported complex-survey weight application; additionally, cross-sectional TIMSS data prevent causal claims.
